Unofficial until approved by the
  Alhambra City Council

  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Council Chambers, 111 South First Street
  August 9, 2021
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:06 p.m., on Monday, August 9, 2021 the Alhambra City Council met in Council
Chambers and virtually via Zoom.

PRESENT:  LEE
PRESENT via Zoom:  MAZA, MALONEY, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present in person and via Zoom: City Manager Binnquist, City Attorney Montes,
Assistant City Manager Garcia, Deputy City Manager Stover, City Clerk Myles, Director of Finance
Lieu, Director of Public Works/ Utilities Ray, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Program
Coordinator Wong, Director of Library LohGuan, Marketing and Communications Specialist
Nguyen, Director of Community Development Ho, Fire Chief Phelps, Police Chief Parra, Director
of Human Resources Ko

CITY CLERK REPORT - NOTICE NO. N2M21-101

The City Clerk hereby reported that she duly gave notice of the regular meeting of the City Council
being held this evening pursuant to the order of the Mayor in accordance with Section 54955 and
54956 of the Government Code of the State of California.

READING OF ORDINANCE TITLES
Government Code Section 36934 requires that all ordinances be read in full prior to City Council
taking action on the ordinance. By listing the ordinance title on the Council agenda, Council may
determine that the title has been read.

Action Taken:  On motion of Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER, seconded by Mr. MAZA, the City
Council determined that the titles to all ordinances which appeared on this public agenda had
been read, and waived further reading. Hearing no objections, the Mayor so ordered.

Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: MAZA
  Ayes:  MAZA, MALONEY, PÉREZ, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

CEREMONIAL

1.  RECOGNITION: ALHAMBRA CERTIFIED FARMER’S MARKET 37th ANNIVERSARY –
  F2M21-3
  3
8-9-21
   Mayor Lee and the Alhambra City Council, on behalf of the citizens of Alhambra, wished
  to recognize and congratulate the Alhambra Certified Farmer’s Market as it celebrated its
  37th anniversary. Established in 1984, the Alhambra Certified Farmer’s Market has
  continued to provide the community with fresh local fruit and produce from certified
  growers in California, as well as honey, herbs, bread, flowers and offers family friendly
  activities every Sunday. The City Council commended the Alhambra Certified Farmer’s
  Market for their service, offered best wishes for its continued success and encouraged all
  to visit the Market to join in the anniversary celebration.

PRESENTATIONS

2.  2021-2029 HOUSING ELEMENT UPDATE OF THE ALHAMBRA GENERAL PLAN –
  F2M20-37

  Director of Community Development HO delivered a staff report and introduced Chris
  BLAKNEY, Project Director from ECONorthwest who presented to the City Council an
  update on the 2021-2029 Housing Element Update Project of the Alhambra General Plan.
  The presentation provided an update and overview of the status and schedule of the
  project, including the Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA). The presentation is
  on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  Public Comment:  Lewis MCCAMMON spoke regarding the State of California’s
  deadline for Housing Element Updates, completion of the Zoning Code Update, and the
  RNHA cycle 5 and 6 numbers as well as completed projects. He spoke in support of the
  process and stressed the need for low and very low housing projects.

  Discussion: Councilmember PÉREZ and Mr. BLAKNEY discussed the community
  outreach plan, the environmental impact of continued building developments with regards
  to issues of infrastructure, and housing access equity. They also discussed the balance
  between the need for affordable housing and the lack of resources needed to develop
  those projects. They discussed programs such as the inclusionary housing ordinance.
  They further discussed broad zoning update ideas such as the elimination of R1 zoning or
  100% Affordable Housing Overlay as well as Alhambra’s consideration of extending the
  density bonus to provide more affordable housing projects.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed residents’ preference for R1 zoning in
  District 5, expansion of Accessory Dwelling Unit development to assist multi-generational
  family living and maintaining a balanced density for each lot, City owned properties that
  could be developed into more affordable housing projects, and the development of Valley
  Boulevard.

  Councilmember MALONEY and Mr. BLAKNEY discussed the proposed strategy to meet
  the State RHNA numbers, the challenges of Alhambra’s parceled community with medium
  scale development and productive uses, and the continued need to identify the optimal
  opportunities to combine lots to create sites which would facilitate housing development.
  They continued to discuss the detailed report which would be delivered to Council for
  future discussion and the ways in which ECONorthwest has compiled a report which would
  meet the State RNHA goals. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. BLAKNEY discussed the
  responsibility of other cities to meet their RNHA goals, the State’s review of housing
  4
8-9-21
   underproduction, State mandates on communities to facilitate housing production, the
  State’s resources offered to cities to assist in housing production, and the development of
  other cities Housing Elements.

  Councilmember MAZA thanked Mr. BLAKNEY for his work and stressed the need for
  continued community outreach.

  Mayor LEE and Mr. BLAKNEY discussed SB9 and the State’s consideration to allow
  additional housing units in R1 zoning, residents’ concerns regarding the alteration of R1
  zoning, and the analysis Alhambra’s ADU program with regards to existing ADU
  application trends and projecting a reasonable development rate for future ADUs. They
  went on to discuss the capacity shortfall data with regards to projects approved or in the
  entitlement process, vacant sites scattered throughout the community, existing
  underutilized sites which were identified in the 5th Cycle Housing Element Inventory but
  were reassessed according to current State requirements, and potential underutilized sites
  which were not previously considered under existing zoning requirements but could be
  made available with proposed changes to density and rezoning. Ms. LEE and Mr.
  BLAKNEY discussed future discussions of overlayed zoning on excess congregational
  land as it could affect the identified potential underutilized housing sites. They went on to
  discuss the East Main Corridor study and potential housing on a particular segment of the
  zone. They also discussed upzoning the downtown corridor to allow for most intensive
  development or the highest density development. Ms. LEE and Mr. BLAKNEY discussed
  the State’s extended deadline and timeline for an adopted Housing Element update as
  well as implementing the changes to the Zoning Code update which would support the
  adopted Housing Element.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed this informational report.

3.  INTRODUCTION TO THE 2021-2022 CITY COUNCIL REDISTRICTING PROCESS –
  F2M21-28

  Andrew WESTALL, Principal with Bear Demographics & Research, Technical Director
  David Ely, and Outreach Director Tizoc DeAztlan provided the City Council with an
  introduction to the 2021-2022 City Council redistricting process which would take place
  after each decennial census. The presentation included a summary of redistricting law,
  criteria, and process. The presentation is on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  Discussion: Councilmember PÉREZ and Mr. WESTALL discussed working with the
  City Attorney and the consultants to use traditional criteria such as contiguity and
  compactness in the redistricting process which would not violate the Voting Rights Act or
  the Equal Protection Clause with regards to race or ethnicity.

  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Mr. WESTALL discussed the next step of
  reviewing the draft map and the public review period for the draft before the meeting. Ms.
  ANDRADE-STADLER and Mr. WESTALL went on to discuss receiving public input from
  each district and public engagement in the map drawing process through community
  workshops, a robust website dedicated to the process, translated materials into various
  languages, live translators at public workshops, and an online mapping tool.

  5
8-9-21
   Councilmember MALONEY and Mr. WESTALL discussed the current district boundaries
  with regards to support from residents, sampling data from the US Census, population
  growth in the City, relation to the Voting Rights Act, and community input.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed this informational report.

4.  DISCUSSION REGARDING THE RESTRUCTURING OF BOARDS AND
  COMMISSIONS INCLUDING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BOARDS AND
  COMMISSIONS – F2M21-36

  Deputy City Manager STOVER delivered a staff report and presentation which is on file in
  the City Clerk’s office. From February through June 2021, in response to objectives
  identified in the City’s 2020-21 Strategic Plan, the City Council discussed a variety of
  changes to the City’s current groups including the installation of new Boards and
  Commissions. Throughout the discussions, the Council focused on changes that will
  further support the needs and public participation priorities of the City. In consideration,
  Board and Commission composition, frequency of meetings, and changes to scope were
  among some of the specific topic points engaged by the Council. The City’s ten existing
  Boards and Commissions included:

  1) Civil Service Commission; 2) Transportation Commission; 3) Arts & Cultural Events
  Committee; 4) Library Board of Trustees; 5) Parks & Recreation Commission; 6) Design
  Review Board; 7) HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee; 8) Environmental Committee; 9)
  Planning Commission; and, 10) Youth Commission. The new Boards and Commissions
  identified throughout recent Council discussions included: 1) Historic Preservation
  Committee; 2) Social Justice and Equity Commission; and, 3) Beautification Commission.
  After much discussion, staff collected notes from the Council meetings and prepared a
  summary of comments and suggestions of the City Council. At this time, staff looked for
  City Council to provide confirmation of the desired changes to the existing Boards and
  Commissions as well as provide final direction on the new Boards, Committees, and
  Commissions to be created. Following the Council’s consensus of the changes to the
  City’s Boards and Commissions, staff would move forward with preparing any formal
  amendments needed to the City’s Municipal Code.

  Public Comment:  Lewis MCCAMMON cited sections from the Alhambra Municipal
  Code regarding the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee. He discussed the difficulties with
  scheduled meetings and multiple cancellations. He further discussed the need for other
  City departments to provide detailed reports to the Committee, as the substance of work
  could fall within the interest of the Committee.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office: Oscar AMARO
  wrote in support of the creation of an Historic Preservation Commission.

  Discussion: Mayor LEE proposed that Council make discuss and vote in the categories
  of age requirements, by district appointment, and meeting frequency rather than
  individually assess each commission. Council discussed and suggested the removal of
  age requirements from all boards and commissions with the exception of the Planning
  Commission, Design Review Board, and the Civil Service Commission which would
  maintain a minimum of 18 years or voting age. Council further discussed and suggested
  6
8-9-21
   the removal of language requiring the elector status of commissioners. Mayor LEE, Deputy
  City Manager STOVER, and City Attorney MONTES briefly discussed the responsibilities
  of the Library Board.

  Council agreed to maintain at large appointments rather than by district as this would allow
  for greater diversity at this time. Council also agreed that no changes would be made to
  the Civil Service Commission with regards to meeting frequency.

  Council next discussed residency requirements and agreed that the requirements should
  be consistent for all Boards and Commissions with the exception of the Planning
  Commission. Council agreed that there should be residency requirements for all Boards
  of Commissions, but that only Planning Commission require a minimum of 1 year
  residency in Alhambra. Councilmember PÉREZ made several points in favor of removing
  the residency minimum requirements by stating that it was possible that an ideal candidate
  would qualify to serve the Planning Commission who may not meet the minimum
  residency requirement. Councilmember MAZA stated that given the types of projects the
  Planning Commission deliberated on, that it was necessary for Commissioners to have
  longstanding knowledge and understanding of Alhambra’s communities. Council agreed
  with Mr. Maza’s comments.

  Council discussed the age requirement for the Youth Commission and ultimately agreed
  to maintain the required limit of 14 – 20 years of age. Mayor LEE spoke in favor of lowering
  the maximum age to 18 due to potentially conflicting schedules of college age students.
  Mr. MAZA stated that the range of 14 – 20 years of age allowed for more potential
  candidates for Councilmembers to choose from and added that should any Commissioner
  not fulfil their duties, Councilmembers could choose to remove that Commissioner.
  Council agreed with Mr. Maza’s comments.

  Council next discussed the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee and the frequency of
  meetings. Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and City Manager BINNQUIST
  discussed the most necessary meetings in April to review funding for the Annual Action
  Plan and in September for the Annual Action Plan which are brought before Council in a
  public hearing. Ms. BINNQUIST explained that the role of the HCDA Committee has
  diminished with the end of the Redevelopment Agency. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER
  discussed other potential areas in which the HCDA Committee could review at other
  monthly meetings such as the draft Housing Element or hosting housing summits for
  residents. Ms. BINNQUIST suggested that if Council would like the committee to review
  other topics, that they be tied to the use of HUD funding and stated that there were
  relatively few opportunities with select funding. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER and Ms.
  BINNQUIST went on to discuss Senior Case Management and Code Enforcement as
  HUD funded projects in which statistical progress reports are provided to the HCDA
  Committee for the purpose of determining continued funding.

  Councilmember PÉREZ discussed Commissioner MCCAMMON’s comments regarding
  additional topics the HCDA Committee could review. She agreed that the City could more
  actively monitor the California Regional Housing Needs Assessment and the
  Accountability Act in order to address the housing crisis in a long-term way. She referred
  to a meeting she attended with the Executive Director of Abundant Housing LA and
  discussed a model used by the Canadian city of Toronto called the Planning Review Panel
  in which 20 randomly selected members from a civic lottery would serve for two years to
  7
8-9-21
   provide input on city planning initiatives in an attempt to provide diverse perspectives on
  housing issues. She pointed out the benefits of this model and the past success of townhall
  meetings in Alhambra. She stated that a model such as this might address the aspirations
  of the HCDA Committee as well as transition the committee into a planning review model
  now that there are no redevelopment issues to oversee. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER and
  Ms. PÉREZ briefly discussed the potential selection process and the ways in which
  random selection could allow for input from groups who may have been overlooked in the
  past.

  Ms. LEE requested more reports from the HCDA Committee to Council and Ms.
  BINNQUIST discussed the Consolidated Annual Performance Evaluation Report
  (CAPER) as well as the Annual Action Plan reports as presented to Council with the
  recorded HCDA Committee votes. Ms. LEE went on to suggest the Committee discuss
  other topics such as the rental units and AirBnB units in Alhambra and report the findings
  to Council. She agreed that the Committee members do not feel participatory and that the
  Council has the means to revive the Committee.

  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER supported further discussion regarding Ms. Pérez’s
  suggestions and requested more information on the topic from staff. Council agreed to
  table further discussion of the HCDA Committee to a future Council meeting following a
  more in-depth report from staff regarding the Planning Review Panel model and other
  potential topics for the Committee to review.

  Council went on to discuss the qualifications for members of the Planning Commission.
  Councilmember MALONEY suggested that they maintain the qualification requirements
  and offer additional training to Planning Commissioners such as provided by the League
  of California Cities. Mr. MONTES clarified that the League’s training seminars are booked
  months and sometimes years in advance and that they may not be frequent enough to
  fully train appointed Planning Commissioners. Ms. BINNQUIST confirmed the difficulties
  in availability and clarified that the City’s contracted law firm Burke, Williams & Sorensen
  had provided similar training to Councilmembers. Mr. MALONEY suggested that this
  training be extended to Planning Commissioners. Ms. LEE agreed with this suggestion
  and also suggested that given the intensive workload and importance of responsibilities,
  a stipend be provided to Planning Commission members. Council supported Mr.
  Maloney’s suggestion for training and did not support a stipend to Planning
  Commissioners as it would be unfair to other Board and Commission members. Mr. MAZA
  suggested that any training occur within 90 days of appointment if logistically possible.

  Council also discussed the Parks and Recreation Commission. Mayor LEE stated that
  there were no quorum issues and that therefore Council could revisit the meeting regularity
  should any issues arise. She suggested that the Mayor could appoint an additional
  eleventh Commissioner who would be either a senior citizen or a youth member to ensure
  greater age diversity in the case that none of the other appointees represent these age
  groups. She reasoned that Senior Citizens were directly affected by Parks and Recreation
  programs and that their interests should be represented on the Commission. Council
  discussed the suggestion, the potential selection process, the challenges for staff to verify
  age of candidates who submit Applications for Civil Service, and the number of retirees
  who currently serve on commissions. Ms. PÉREZ suggested that the perhaps the
  commissioner requirements could stress the importance of age diversity in Council
  selections. Mr. MAZA supported Ms. Lee’s suggestion and made the additional suggestion
  8
8-9-21
   that one Councilmember attend commission meetings on a rotating basis and report back
  to the rest of Council. He stated that he believed that the Parks and Recreation
  Commission could have a more active role. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER supported Ms.
  Lee and Mr. Maza’s suggestions.

  Council discussed changes to the Environmental Committee. Mr. MALONEY suggested
  changing the name to the Environmental Sustainability Commission and further discussed
  the need to change the scope to embrace a new emphasis on issues of sustainability. He
  stated that the Committee was poised to become a centerpiece to provide feedback from
  the community to Council and that its importance should be emphasized going forward.
  He further suggested that the Committee could meet monthly or bimonthly and requested
  that staff provide a monthly report on the activities of the Clean Power Alliance to the
  Committee. Council supported Mr. MALONEY’s suggestions. Mr. MONTES and Ms. LEE
  discussed the need to establish the Commission via an ordinance to the Alhambra
  Municipal Code rather than its previous resolution. Council supported changing the name
  to Environmental Sustainability Commission, bimonthly regular meetings, updating the
  duties as outlined in the staff report, and establishing the committee via Ordinance.

  RECESS & RECONVENE: Mayor LEE called for a brief recess at 9:45 p.m. and the
  meeting resumed with all Councilmembers present at 9:55 p.m.

  Council resumed with a discussion regarding the creation of a new Historic Preservation
  Commission. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER suggested keeping the recommended name of
  Historic Preservation Commission, that membership be limited to five members, that
  meetings be monthly, that elector status not be required, that residency in Alhambra be
  required, and that potential commissioners would demonstrate a knowledge of history and
  perhaps understand California and United States preservation resources. Ms. PÉREZ
  agreed with Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s recommendations and further suggested that staff
  review language establishing duties for the West Hollywood Historic Preservation
  Commission. She cited duties such as periodically updating the Historic Resources Survey
  and making recommendations to the Planning Commission and City Council. She also
  suggested that staff research the California State Office of Historic Preservation to ensure
  that the Commission would be compliant with guidelines under the office’s Certified Local
  Government Programs. Mr. MALONEY and Mr. MAZA agreed with Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s
  and Ms. Pérez’s suggestions. Mr. MAZA added that the commission could meet monthly
  initially, and then reassess once their work with the Historic Resources Survey has been
  concluded. Mr. MONTES, Ms. LEE, and Ms. BINNQUIST discussed the process in
  drafting the Historic Context Assessment, the Historic Preservation Ordinance, and the
  Historic Resources Survey with regards as to when the Historic Preservation Commission
  would be created and whether or not their duties would be advisory or decision making.
  Mr. MAZA suggested that the Commission be created after the Context Assessment has
  been concluded so that the commission would have context to work from. Ms. LEE and
  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER next discussed the relationship between the Commission and
  the Alhambra Historical Museum and Society. Ms. PÉREZ and Mr. MALONEY supported
  the City continue with plans to circulate a Request for Proposals for a group to manage
  the museum and its assets separate from the Commission, but agreed that the
  Commission may have some involvement in the museum.

  Council next discussed the creation of a Social Justice and Equity Commission. Ms.
  ANDRADE-STADLER suggested changing the name to the “Human Relations
  9
8-9-21
   Commission,” explaining that the United States Department of Justice had provided
  guidelines for local governments to create such a commission. She suggested that the
  mission would be to promote ways in which communities could get along and foster
  goodwill which could be provided through cultural literacy. She suggested that the
  commission be an advisory commission who could help conduct research to draft a report
  card for the City and would point out areas which needed improvement. She suggested
  that the commission have ten meetings who would attend monthly meetings, that
  residency be required, and that a Councilmember attend meetings on a rotational basis.
  She further discussed potential areas of interest for the commission such as criminal
  justice, government, business and economic development, hate crime, conflict
  management, education, employment, and cultural literacy or expression. She suggested
  that staff review the City of Pasadena’s Human Relations Commission.

  Mayor LEE and Ms. BINNQUIST discussed which department would oversee the
  commission. Ms. LEE questioned the specific duties of the commission given the broad
  topics discussed. Ms. PÉREZ agreed with Ms. Andrade-Stadler’s suggestion of the name
  and suggested ways in which the commission could address equity such as reviewing the
  diversity of City staff hires, the promotion of women and women of color in City positions,
  provide resources to recent immigrants, and review COVID-19 vaccination rates by district
  to reach underserved groups. She expressed that the Commission had great potential
  with endless options. Mr. MALONEY supported the creation of the commission and the
  name ‘Human Relations Commission.” He expressed that given the broad topics of
  interest, that the commission be allowed to evolve as our ideas of equity and social justice
  continue to evolve and that therefore many aspects of the commission would be flexible.

  Council continued to discuss the potential mission and scope of the Commission. Mr.
  MAZA suggested forming the commission with five members and bimonthly meetings and
  then reconsidering the size and frequency as participation grows. After further discussion,
  Council requested that staff present a report with draft language from the Pasadena’s
  Human Relations Commission or the Los Angeles County’s Human Relations
  Commission.

  Council next addressed their previous suggestion of a Beautification Commission. Council
  reached a consensus that since many of the goals which inspired this commission were
  currently in progress and since many of the duties could be shared by already established
  commissions, that they would not move forward with this commission.

  Mr. MALONEY revisited previous discussion regarding providing a stipend to
  Commissioners and suggested an alternate means of expressing appreciation to the hard
  work of Commissioners, such as an event. Mayor LEE agreed with the suggestion.

  Action Taken:  City Council confirmed the proposed restructuring changes to the
  City’s Boards and Commissions including the establishment of new Boards and
  Commissions, and provided additional direction in discussion for staff to undertake the
  steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.

5.  COVID REOPENING UPDATE – F2M20-33

  City Manager BINNQUIST provided updates to the City Council on reopening since the
  10
8-9-21
   last update provided at the August 3, 2021 meeting. Topics included: City operations, City
  Council and Boards and Commission meetings; various agencies at the Federal, State,
  County and City levels requiring employees to be vaccinated; and, Alhambra’s community
  and City employee vaccination rates.

  Public Comment:  Lewis MCCAMMON reported on the press release from the Los
  Angeles County Health Department regarding hospitalization rates for COVID-19 among
  unvaccinated individuals. He further reported on new cases of COVID-19 in Alhambra,
  continued vaccinations, and the beginning of the school year.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office:
  The following people wrote to oppose vaccine mandates and passports:

  1) Michael Briel
  2) Jayne Chen

  Additional comment:

  3) Cody Corbett wrote against continued City Council meetings via zoom and supported
  holding public City Council meetings on the lawn area outside of City Hall. He included
  a list of other residents who also supported this suggestion.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER discussed how the rise in COVID-
  19 cases has affected at-home remote learning for grade school and middle school
  students. She went on to state that while Alhambra was admirable in providing early
  vaccinations to employees and while a 70% vaccination rate was good, that it was still a
  low percentage. She supported continued testing sites. Ms. ANDRADE_STADLER and
  Ms. BINNQUIST discussed unvaccinated staff who continued to work with the public, the
  percentage of unvaccinated staff in the Police and Fire departments, exceptions due to
  religious reasons, and Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER’s concerns with regard to unvaccinated
  staff members such as paramedics who interact directly with the public. She suggested
  continuing to make vaccinations widely accessible in an attempt to persuade more
  employees to receive vaccinations.

  Councilmember PÉREZ discussed offering weekly COVID tests to unvaccinated
  employees. She acknowledged the hesitancy of some to receive the vaccine and added
  that the City needed to continue their due diligence to continue testing in light of ongoing
  COVID variant strains. She agreed with Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER that the City needed
  to avoid risk of infection to the public.

  Councilmember MALONEY discussed the importance of the vaccine for those that were
  able to receive it, the risk of virus mutation among unvaccinated individuals, and supported
  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER’s suggestion of making vaccinations as accessible as possible.

  Councilmember MAZA discussed the threat of COVID-19, the City’s effectiveness in
  addressing each change and challenge, reaching the 77% vaccination rate and the choice
  of the remaining population to abstain from the vaccine, and the City’s need to continue
  adapting to each new change.

  Ms. PÉREZ discussed Mr. Corbett’s comments regarding issues with Zoom and the need
  11
8-9-21
   for the City to address their concerns regarding accessibility.

  Mayor LEE discussed breakthrough infections among vaccinated individuals, supported
  Ms. Pérez’s suggestion of providing weekly testing for all employees regardless of
  vaccination status due to the possibility of breakthrough infections, and the possibility of a
  booster shot to the vaccine. Ms. LEE and MS. BINNQUIST discussed the current testing
  process for employees. Ms. LEE went on to stress the need to continue regular testing for
  employees, monitoring case studies and infection rates, encouraging vaccination for
  employees by talking to union representation, State guidelines regarding those with
  negative reactions to the vaccine, and mandatory sick days given to those with negative
  reactions to the vaccine. She also discussed concerns regarding meeting accessibility and
  the possibility of outdoor in-person public meetings in front of City Hall. Ms. BINNQUIST
  stated that she would look into whether or not the City had the appropriate technological
  and logistic infrastructure to hold large outdoor public meetings. City Attorney MONTES
  stated that the City was complying with all legal requirements in providing adequate
  access and that addressing technological concerns was an education process.

  Mr. MALONEY and Ms. BINNQUIST discussed the ability of the public to use toll free
  phone numbers to connect to the meetings. Mr. MALONEY and Ms. PÉREZ made
  suggestions to provide reminders during the meeting on how to navigate Zoom either
  online or via phone.

  Ms. LEE continued to discuss her suggestion to hold outdoor in-person meetings.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed this informational report.

CONSENT AGENDA (Item Nos. 6 – 26)

All items listed under the Consent Agenda, with the exception of Item Nos. 7, 13, 23, and 26,
were considered by the City Council to be routine and were enacted by one motion.

6.  APPROPRIATE FUNDS: PURCHASE AND TRAINING OF POLICE SERVICE DOG –
  F2M21-17, M2M21-95

  On July 12, 2021, the Police Department’s sole Police Service Dog, “Mitch,” was medically
  retired and the City Council authorized the sale of Mitch to a private party. The Canine
  Unit of the Police Field Services Division, Patrol Section, is an intrinsic section of the
  division. The Canine Unit supports the department in achieving their goals by training and
  certifying this asset to perform tasks not humanly possible due to the dog’s scent detecting
  capability. Therefore, staff requested that the City Council appropriate funds for the
  purchase and training of a Police Service Dog. Expenditures included approximately
  $13,230 for the purchase of a Police Service Dog and $5,700 for canine handling and
  canine certification.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council appropriated funds in the amount of $18,930 for the
  purchase of a Police Service Dog (canine) and necessary training; and, directed staff to
  undertake the steps necessary to finalize the Council’s action. (M2M21-95)
  12
8-9-21
   Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: PÉREZ
  Ayes:  PÉREZ, MAZA, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, LEE
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

7.  TERMINATION OF THE FOOTHILL AIR SUPPORT TEAM (FAST) PROGRAM –
  F2M1-33, C2M1-16, M2M21-96

  On February 12, 2001 the City Council officially joined the Foothill Air Support Team
  (FAST) program under a mutually agreed Joint Powers of Authority (JPA) for Police
  Helicopter Services. The FAST program (helicopter overwatch) was a consistent asset to
  the community of Alhambra and a vital officer safety tool for the officers of the Alhambra
  Police Department, but upon further analysis of the yearly current financial obligation, the
  APD proposed conducting a search of more cost-effective helicopter solutions/programs.
  The JPA agreement stated any agency may terminate/withdraw from the program at the
  end of any given fiscal year and to do so in writing to all the participating agencies not less

  The Alhambra Municipal Code required placement of long-term overnight parking permits
  in the rear window of vehicles. However, instructions on the City’s application for parking
  permits indicated placement should be in the lower left corner (driver’s side) of the front
  windshield. The windshield was the preferred placement for ease of viewing, since many
  rear windows are tinted. The attached ordinance would provide consistency between the
  application and the code. Additionally, the existing code had provisions concerning
  inspections during the application and renewal processes. Such inspections were not
  currently undertaken, so the attached ordinance would delete those provisions.

  Public Comment received via email on file in the City Clerk’s office: Lewis
  MCCAMMON wrote in support of the ordinance and to suggest additional public outreach.
